title: LRU cache
sub: A dictionary finds, a list keeps the order: O(1) Get and Put, and the same cache on indices with no allocations
cards/0/title: The problem and the signals of a design task
cards/0/body:
LRU Cache (LeetCode #146). Design a class with a capacity capacity and two methods: Get(key) returns the value or −1, Put(key, value) inserts the key or updates its value. When there are more keys than capacity, evict the one that has gone unused the longest (least recently used). Both Get and Put count as a use: each makes the key the most recent. Both operations are O(1) on average. Constraints: capacity ≤ 3000, keys ≤ 10⁴, up to 2·10⁵ calls.

There is no input here — there are methods. This is a data structure design problem, and it has its own signals:

1. “Implement the class …”, a list of calls with expected outputs — choose the state first (which dictionaries, lists, counters), then write the methods.
2. “O(1) per operation” — no method may contain a single pass over the data.
3. “Evict the least …” — you need two structures: one that finds (a dictionary) and one that keeps order.

LRU is the most common design problem in both .NET and Unity interviews: every service and every engine has a cache.
cards/1/q: Capacity 2. Calls: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Put(1, 10), Put(3, 3), Get(1), Get(2). What do the last two Gets return?
cards/1/explain: Put(1, 10) is an update and also a use: key 1 became more recent than key 2. Put(3, 3) does not fit and evicts the least recent key — 2. Get(1) returns the new value 10, Get(2) returns −1.
cards/1/wrong/1: That would happen if an update did not count as a use: key 1 would stay the least recent. But by the statement a Put is a use too.
cards/1/wrong/2: A Put on an existing key replaces the value: after Put(1, 10) it holds 10, not 1.
cards/1/wrong/3: With capacity 2 there would be three keys: Put(3, 3) has to evict someone. That is key 2 — it was used least recently.
cards/2/body:
Dictionary + timestamp. Store key → (value, tick), where tick is the number of the last use from a global counter. Get is O(1). But to evict you have to find the smallest tick — a scan over all keys, O(capacity). If every Put evicts, that is 2·10⁵ · 3000 = 6·10⁸ operations — seconds.

Dictionary + a List<int> for order. The most recent key goes to the end of the list, the victim is list[0]. But using a key from the middle means list.Remove(key): a linear search and a shift of the tail, O(n). And RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole list as well.

SortedSet<(long tick, int key)>. The minimum is O(log n), a use is Remove of the old pair and Add of a new one, O(log n). A working answer, and worth saying out loud, but the statement asks for O(1), and every tree node is an allocation.

All three share one flaw: they search for the recency order instead of keeping it. We need a structure where moving a known element to the front and removing from the back cost O(1).
cards/3/q: The “dictionary + List<int> for order” solution: on every Get the key moves to the end — list.Remove(key), then list.Add(key). 2·10⁵ calls, capacity 3000. What is wrong?
cards/3/options/0: Remove(key) searches for the key linearly and shifts the tail: O(capacity) per call, up to 6·10⁸ operations
cards/3/options/1: Nothing: Remove and Add on a List<T> are O(1)
cards/3/options/2: List<int> boxes every key, which creates garbage
cards/3/options/3: Only RemoveAt(0) on eviction is a problem; Remove(key) is cheap
cards/3/explain: A List<T> is an array: Remove(key) first looks for the value linearly (IndexOf), then shifts everything to its right with Array.Copy. Both steps are O(n). Over 2·10⁵ calls with 3000 keys that is on the order of 6·10⁸ operations, and the task asked for O(1).
cards/3/wrong/1: List<T> is O(1) only for Add at the end, the indexer and removing the last element. Remove(value) is a search plus a shift, O(n).
cards/3/wrong/2: List<int> stores ints in an int[] without boxing. The problem is the scan, not garbage.
cards/3/wrong/3: RemoveAt(0) is O(n) too, but Remove(key) is no cheaper: it searches for the key and shifts the tail.
cards/4/body:
A doubly linked list keeps the recency order: the most recent key at the front, the next one to go at the back. Moving a node to the front and removing the last one cost O(1) once the node is in hand. The dictionary key → LinkedListNode puts it in your hand: this is the pairing from the linked list unit, where nodes are stored outside the list.

Get: find the node in the dictionary → unlink it → insert it at the front → return the value.
Put: the key exists — unlink its old node. The key is new and the cache is full — remove the last node and delete its key from the dictionary. Then insert (key, value) at the front and store the node in the dictionary.

Two details people get wrong. The node stores the key as well: on eviction you hold the last node, and you must delete its key from the dictionary. And the order of checks: first “does the key exist”, and only for a new key — eviction; an update does not change the size.

Invariant: the dictionary and the list hold the same keys, and the list is ordered from most to least recent. Every method restores this before returning. Time is O(1) on average per operation (average because of the dictionary), memory is O(capacity).
cards/4/flow/3: new key and full → drop the tail
cards/4/flow/4: tail's key → out of the dictionary
cards/5/explain: Remove(node) is O(1): the node comes from the dictionary. Remove(key) would not even compile here (the list holds tuples), and LinkedList<T>.Remove(value) is a scan. else if: evict only for a new key, an update does not change the size. The victim is the tail of the list, order.Last, and you delete its key from the dictionary, not its value.
cards/6/task: Walk the trace: capacity 3. The most recent key is on the left, the next to go is on the right. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Update the value and move 3 to the front: 3, 1, 2
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Evict 2 from the tail, then insert 3
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Change the value and leave 3 where it is: 1, 3, 2
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: The list is 1, 3, 2. The cache is full, and put(3, 30) arrives — key 3 is already there. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The key exists, so this is an update: the size does not change and nobody needs to go. The code unlinks the old node 3 and inserts (3, 30) at the front: a Put is a use too. “Evict 2” is exactly the order-of-checks bug: eviction is only for a new key.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: The list is 3, 4, 1. put(5, 5) is a new key and the cache is full. Whom does the code evict?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: The victim is the tail of the list, order.Last: no search needed. It is key 1: it was last touched by get(1) at the very start, and since then 3 (update), 4 (insert) and 3 again were used. The node leaves the list, and its key 1 leaves the dictionary.
cards/7/q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Put(2, 5), Get(1). Get returned −1, but it should return 1. Tap the buggy line.
cards/7/explain: Eviction is checked before “does the key exist”. Put(2, 5) sees a full cache and drops the tail — key 1 — even though it is an update and there is enough room. The fix is the order: TryGetValue first, and eviction in an else if, only for a new key.
cards/8/title: LinkedList<T> or your own list on indices
cards/8/body:
What the solution above costs. Every AddFirst((key, value)) is a new LinkedListNode object: a 16-byte header, three references and the tuple — 48 bytes on 64-bit. It is created both for a new key and on every update. The node can be reused: AddFirst(node) accepts a node that is already unlinked, and the value changes through node.Value. Then a new object is needed only for a new key, and on eviction you can take the removed tail. But the nodes are still scattered across the heap: every hop is a cache miss, and the Boehm GC walks all of them on every collection.

A list on indices (linked list unit): keys, values and the prev/next links live in arrays, and a “node” is a slot number. Slot 0 is a sentinel: next[0] is the most recent, prev[0] the least recent, and an empty list is the sentinel looped onto itself. There are no null checks at all. Eviction takes the tail's slot and gives it to the new key.

All the arrays and the dictionary are created in the constructor. A dictionary with a preset capacity does not grow, and it reuses removed entries through its own free list. So after the constructor there are zero allocations on any call. The arrays can move to a NativeArray, but the dictionary is managed: in Burst a NativeHashMap<int, int> replaces it.
cards/8/deep:
Threads. Two structures change together, so a ConcurrentDictionary does not help: between the dictionary edit and the list edit another thread sees them out of sync. You need one lock around the whole method — Get included: a read moves a node, so it writes. A reader–writer lock buys nothing here. Under load the cache is split into N independent shards by hash(key) % N, each with its own lock: the eviction order becomes approximate, but threads barely wait for each other.

.NET has no ready-made LRU. OrderedDictionary<TKey, TValue> from .NET 9 keeps insertion order in an array: moving a key out of the middle is a removal with a shift, O(n). MemoryCache from Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Memory is not an LRU: if a new entry does not fit into SizeLimit, it is simply not added, and the cache compacts in the background by a CompactionPercentage share — expired entries first, then by priority, and only within a priority by recency.

Approximations. Strict LRU pays for a reorder on every read. The CLOCK algorithm keeps entries in a ring buffer with a “touched” bit: a read only sets the bit, and on eviction a hand walks the ring, clears bits and takes the first entry without one. Variants of CLOCK replace pages in operating systems and buffers in databases. Redis evicts by sampling: it picks a few random keys and removes the least recent of them.
cards/9/q: What is true about the two LRU implementations? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: In the first version, a Put on an existing key creates a new node: order.AddFirst((key, value))
cards/9/options/1: The node can be reused: change node.Value and insert the same node with AddFirst(node)
cards/9/options/2: The index version allocates no memory on any call after the constructor
cards/9/options/3: LinkedList<T>.Remove(value) is O(1) too, so storing the node in the dictionary is optional
cards/9/options/4: The index version can be called from a Burst job as is
cards/9/explain: AddFirst(T value) always creates a new LinkedListNode, while AddFirst(node) inserts an existing one, and after Remove a node is free to be inserted again. In the index version all arrays and the dictionary with a capacity are created up front, and the dictionary reuses removed entries. Remove(value) is a scan, O(n). And Burst cannot touch a managed Dictionary: the arrays move to NativeArray, the dictionary to NativeHashMap.
cards/10/title: Unity: an asset cache evicts by memory
cards/10/body:
Games cache textures, meshes and audio loaded from Addressables or from disk. The limit here is not the number of entries but memory: a 4096×4096 RGBA32 texture is 64 MB (mipmaps add another third), a 64×64 icon is 16 KB. “At most 100 entries” guarantees nothing.

It is the same LRU, but each entry has a weight in bytes, and the cache keeps the total bytes and a budget. Insertion: add at the front, add the weight, then in a loop drop the tail while bytes > budget — several entries may go. An entry heavier than the whole budget is not cached at all: it would evict everything and still not fit.

What matters in Unity. You compute the weight yourself on load: width × height × bytes per pixel of the format (compressed formats use less than a byte per pixel). Profiler.GetRuntimeMemorySizeLong returns 0 when the profiler is not available — and a release build has none. Evicting means releasing: Addressables.Release(handle) for something loaded, Destroy for a texture created in code. The GC knows nothing about a texture's native memory: dropping the reference does not free it — the texture lives on until Destroy or Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets. And whatever is on screen right now is not kept in the eviction list: an entry goes there when its use count drops to zero.
cards/11/q: A texture cache has a 256 MB budget, 250 MB in use. At the tail of the list are three 4 MB textures, and in front of them one of 64 MB. A Put of a new 16 MB texture arrives. What happens?
cards/11/options/0: The three 4 MB textures go: 266 → 254 MB
cards/11/options/1: One texture goes — the least recent
cards/11/options/2: The 64 MB texture goes: that frees the most
cards/11/options/3: The new one is refused: it does not fit the budget right now
cards/11/explain: After the insertion it is 266 MB > 256. The loop drops the tail: 262, then 258 — still over budget — then 254, and the loop stops. The 64 MB texture is more recent, so it stays.
cards/11/wrong/1: One entry is the count-based LRU rule. By memory you evict in a loop until the total fits the budget: 262 MB is still too much.
cards/11/wrong/2: LRU picks by recency, not by weight. The heaviest entry may have been needed a frame ago.
cards/11/wrong/3: Only entries heavier than the whole budget are refused. 16 MB is less than 256: eviction makes the room.
cards/12/q: You are solving LRU Cache out loud in an interview. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: what counts as a use, what to return on a miss, the capacity, whether several threads access it
cards/12/items/1: Name the naive solution: a dictionary with timestamps, eviction by scan — O(capacity)
cards/12/items/2: The idea: a dictionary finds the node, a doubly linked list keeps the recency order
cards/12/items/3: Write Get and Put, stating the invariant: the dictionary and the list hold the same keys
cards/12/items/4: Walk an example with capacity 2: a key update and a tail eviction
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(1) on average per operation, O(capacity) memory
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: a Put on an existing key when the cache is full, capacity 1
cards/12/explain: Agree on the rules first (is a Put a use, what to return, threads), then the baseline, the two-structure idea, code with the invariant, a walk on a small example, complexity and edge cases. An example with an update on a full cache also catches the order-of-checks bug.
cards/13/q: Match each operation with how the LRU cache does it and at what cost.
cards/13/pairs/1/0: Make a key the most recent
cards/13/pairs/2/1: order.Last — the tail of the list
cards/13/pairs/4/0: A texture cache with a budget
cards/13/pairs/4/1: Drop the tail while bytes > budget
